transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-03 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee, Priya Natarajan, Ethan Cho (Redwood); Carlos Mendes, Sofia Ruiz, Maya Patel, Jamal Ortiz (LumaSense)

00:00 Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we wanted to keep this tight 45 ish minutes and make sure we walk through the scoring table and then decisions. Priya and Ethan are on the results.
00:18 Carlos Mendes: yep thanks, Jordan. Quick note, we had a half hour internal on the sampling script so we might have one or two follow up questions about the dataset parity.
00:28 Priya Natarajan: Great, I'll cover the perf numbers first. Quick reminder: baseline is FP16 on Dedicated, then INT8 and FP8 variants we ran on the same workloads.
00:40 Priya Natarajan: So, median p95 latency - baseline FP16 was 72ms per token, INT8 bumped to 58ms, FP8 was 54ms on the same hardware profile; throughput improved with batching but we kept tiny batch size for latency realism.
00:58 Sofia Ruiz: Sorry one sec, when you say 54ms is that single request cold start included or steady state?
01:05 Priya Natarajan: That's steady state, cold start adds another ~120, but we have warm pools in the pilot configuration so steady numbers are what matter for user‑facing latency.
01:16 Ethan Cho: Also worth flagging the KV cache behavior — we saw some variance with long conversations, INT8 had a slight blow up in memory pressure causing occasional 5‑10% token latency spikes. The transcriber here might show K V cash instead of KV cache, so apologies for transcription.
01:34 Maya Patel: When you say regression, how frequent were hallucination or factuality drops? We surfaced a few user complaints in the ticketing.
01:42 Priya Natarajan: Good question. From the automatic evals, most prompts showed <1.5% accuracy drop comparing INT8 to FP16. But there are clusters where drop is 6‑8% notably for long‑form code synthesis and some multi‑step reasoning prompts.
01:58 Carlos Mendes: That matches what we saw — the internal metric we use (semantic match scorer) shows a mode shift on about 3% of high‑value prompts.
02:07 Jordan Lee: Let's call those the "hotspots". Priya, can you point to the example IDs?
02:12 Priya Natarajan: Yes, I uploaded a spreadsheet — link in the chat — it has top 50 regressions with tokens, golden outputs, and model outputs. I'll email the direct link after.
02:22 Carlos Mendes: We need to make sure those examples are representative of production traffic, not synthetic.
02:27 Priya Natarajan: Understood. A note: some of the variance appears to be prompt formatting sensitive — small whitespace/tokenization differences magnify quantization error.
02:39 Jamal Ortiz: From a security/compliance angle, if we move to Dedicated or Private for the pilot, what's the KMS flow? We've got to keep keys on our side; we can't have the root keys in a shared cloud tenancy.
02:51 Jordan Lee: Good point. For Private we can support customer‑managed KMS/HSM and we have a documented flow; Jordan to follow up with the Private team on the precise HSM integrations and share it.
03:02 Maya Patel: Also SLA question — if we rely on FP8 for the fastest latency but see regressions on critical prompts, what's the fallback? Canary?
03:10 Ethan Cho: We have automatic fallback routing: if prompt ID in hotlist or if quality validator confidence below threshold, route to a higher precision model or a warm FP16 replica in a different capacity tier. That adds a latency delta but is safe.
03:21 Sofia Ruiz: What's the observed delta when fallback happens, ballpark?
03:24 Ethan Cho: Fallback to FP16 adds about 60‑80ms median extra; to a separate regional warm pool could be more due to cross‑region, but you can set policy to avoid cross‑region for critical flows.
03:36 Carlos Mendes: Could we do per‑customer or per‑route policy? Some customers are okay with slight accuracy loss but others want no regression.
03:42 Jordan Lee: Yes, routing policies are configurable per route and per‑API key. That was one of the selling points for Dedicated: fine grained control.
03:50 Priya Natarajan: Back to quality: FP8 actually performed very close to FP16 on many classification prompts; INT8 had the most variance. We ran calibration passes and tried mixed precision blends which recovered some hotspots.
04:06 Maya Patel: Mixed precision blends? Can you expand briefly — what does that mean operationally?
04:10 Priya Natarajan: Sure — we can run the early layers in FP16 and the attention/key‑value kernels in INT8, or selectively quantize only feedforward weights. It's more compile work but reduces regressions.
04:22 Carlos Mendes: That sounds promising but more engineering overhead. Any impact on throughput?
04:27 Priya Natarajan: Small hit — a few percent on throughput, but often latency is still better than baseline due to overall smaller memory footprint.
04:35 Jamal Ortiz: Encryption question again — for Private, will traces and audit logs contain PII? We need to redact before they leave our VPC.
04:44 Jordan Lee: For Private or VPC, logs can be stored in customer account and redacted at the customer side. For Hosted, we have retention controls and redaction tools but we can provide SOC2 docs.
04:54 Jamal Ortiz: Please, send the SOC2 + ISO certs and the log retention policy.
05:00 Jordan Lee: Will do — Jordan to attach in follow up.
05:06 Carlos Mendes: Back to the numbers — is there an easy way to see the perf vs quality tradeoff table?
05:10 Priya Natarajan: Yes the spreadsheet has columns: prompt_id, baseline_score, int8_score, fp8_score, p50/p95 latencies, discovered root cause notes. I'm going to highlight 6 representative cases now.
05:28 05:28 Priya Natarajan: Case A: long code synthesis — INT8 drop 7.9% on semantic match, FP8 drop 2.1%. Latency improved ~22% vs FP16.
05:40 05:40 Carlos Mendes: For code we prefer correctness > latency.
05:43 Jordan Lee: So consensus: code synthesis route should be routed to FP16 or FP8 with careful calibration, not plain INT8.
05:50 Maya Patel: For our customer‑facing chat use case, average convo length is 6 turns, we care p95 latency under 200ms. Are we within that on FP8?
05:59 Priya Natarajan: With small batch and warm pools, p95 is around 180ms on FP8 in your region test. INT8 hovered ~165ms but with the regression caveat.
06:10 Sofia Ruiz: Is there a way to do A/B within the same user session to measure real user impact without risking full rollout?
06:16 Ethan Cho: Yes, canary A/B by percentage and sticky‑session steering. Also we can do user sampling on low‑risk users to gather UX signal.
06:24 Carlos Mendes: Okay, so what's the next checkpoint? More data or switch policy?
06:28 Jordan Lee: Proposed: two parallel tracks — 1) triage top 50 regressions and try mixed precision patches; 2) run a staged canary for 10% of traffic with monitoring and auto rollback. Aim for next checkpoint on Monday.
06:44 Maya Patel: Monday is tight, can we do end of next week?
06:47 Jordan Lee: Let's target 2026-03-09 for the next check, that gives a week for triage.
06:53 Carlos Mendes: Works for us.
06:56 Priya Natarajan: I'll also include a sensitivity analysis — how small prompt changes affect quant error — so you can see the brittleness.
07:06 Jamal Ortiz: For compliance we will need an architecture diagram for Private deploy and key flow.
07:12 Jordan Lee: Action noted, Jordan will share architecture and KMS flow.
07:18 Sophia Ruiz: small note, our infra team is worried about memory fragmentation with INT8 kernels, is that something you can instrument?
07:25 Ethan Cho: Yes, we've got profiler traces and we'll add a run with long conversation memory profiling and share heap dumps with sanitized traces.
07:34 Speaker 1: [inaudible]...
07:37 Jordan Lee: Ok wrapping up, quick recap: Priya to send top‑50 regression spreadsheet and sensitivity analysis, Ethan to add memory & KV cache profiler traces, Jordan to send pricing and Private KMS diagram, Carlos to confirm dataset parity. Next sync 2026‑03‑09.
07:56 Maya Patel: Thanks everyone.
07:58 Jordan Lee: Thanks all, we'll follow up in email.
08:01 End of recording.

Notes on transcript: there are occasional transcription errors (e.g., K V cash for KV cache, Sophia spelled as Sofia sometimes) and speaker attribution on one short segment shows generic Speaker 1. This is expected.
